source.title: A Universal Vibe? Finding and Controlling Language-Agnostic Informal Register with SAEs
source.authors: Uri Z. Kialy; Avraham Shtarkberg; Ayal Klein

record.tranche_reason: The study applies SAE feature analysis to a real multilingual LLM and tests whether extracted features track and causally influence informal register. It extends the subject to an LLM setting, rather than reproducing the original toy-network method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE feature discrimination, cross-language overlap and geometry, and steering outcomes; these bear on V4. Its discussion of SAEs mitigating polysemanticity is background, not a result. The study does not test capacity pressure, feature importance trade-offs, or superposition in toy networks.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs as a tool to locate slang-associated features and steer formality in Gemma-2-9B-IT. Its question is whether informal register is shared across languages, not whether the model stores features in superposition. It has no neuron-level baseline, no check of SAE reconstruction or completeness, and no capacity analysis. Its results bear on register representation, not on any version. The finding that SAE features are interpretable and steerable is presupposed by the method rather than tested against an alternative.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that Gemma-2-9B-IT encodes informal register through a partly shared, abstract pragmatic representation alongside many language-specific features. Its small, geometrically coherent cross-linguistic SAE core causally modulates formality in three source languages and transfers zero-shot to six held-out languages. They caution that the subspace is associated with register rather than fully content-abstract, and may be English-anchored.
record.recipe_differences: The study probes and steers SAE features in one pretrained instruction-tuned LLM, rather than testing toy networks under feature-capacity pressure or reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares Layer 9 and Layer 20: the deeper core has higher geometric coherence, while Layer 9 steering correlations are somewhat larger in magnitude for the three source languages. It also reports that coherence and steering efficacy do not necessarily increase together.

fits_no_version.finding: Gemma-2-9B-IT has a small cross-linguistic SAE feature core for informal register. It is 9-10 features in the top-100 lists of all three languages, against a null max of 7. Its decoder vectors cluster (island score 4.3x at L9, 7.8x at L20), and steering with it shifts formality in 3 source and 6 zero-shot languages; random features do not.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multilingual LLMs encode informal register partly through language-shared SAE features that causally control output formality.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Only Gemma-2-9B-IT is studied. The authors note that layer selection was constrained by pretrained SAE availability and that a comprehensive layer sweep and testing across architectures or scales remain open. Formality judgments rely primarily on GPT-4o-mini; human validation covers 30 completions per language for four languages, with only moderate overall agreement (r = 0.62). The authors also note English-centric bias, occasional language switching, and possible semantic, topical, affective, and social-stance confounds in the slang–literal contrast.
record.rows_left_out: The full per-language top-10 feature tables (Appendix B, Tables 6 and 8) and the full top-token listings for selected feature vectors (Appendix C, Table 9) are not entered as separate rows; the core feature-quality and cross-language results are represented in r1–r14. Additional Layer 9 and bilingual-exclusive steering correlations (Appendices H and J) are omitted because they are supplementary steering conditions beyond the primary Layer 20 results; the paper reports that Layer 9 reproduces the qualitative pattern and gives the bilingual-exclusive correlations in Appendix J.

untested.parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep or geometry of superposed features.
No capacity or importance analysis of polysemanticity.
No analysis of the origins of polysemantic neurons.
No neuron-level comparison showing features spread across neurons. SAE recoverability is assumed via pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs, not tested (no reconstruction, sparsity or dense-probe comparison).
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability across SAEs or canonicality.
No test of feature dimensionality. A 10-feature averaged direction is steered, but 1-D versus multi-D is not examined.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V4 and labelled them 'supports'. That overstates the link: the paper's mention of SAEs mitigating polysemanticity is background. Its results concern register sharing across languages, obtained with pretrained SAEs as an instrument. A curator could argue that the precise single features (e.g. 93521, precision 0.966) weakly illustrate that SAEs recover interpretable directions. The study offers no comparison with neurons or dense directions, though, so that would at most be uses-without-test. There is a single model, and the formality judge is GPT-4o-mini (human agreement r=0.62).

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions; overlapping nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether polysemanticity arises from competition for limited capacity, or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE-recovered features in Gemma-2-9B-IT, but not whether features are spread across neurons, whether this generalizes to other models, or whether the recovered feature set is exhaustive.
Completeness, stability, or canonical status of SAE features as the model’s units.
Whether represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.operation_detail: Used individual Layer 20 SAE features as binary slang classifiers (active means slang) on the pooled cross-linguistic dataset.

conditions.value: pooled English, Hebrew, and Russian; 5,256 slang and 7,697 literal subword tokens

rows.measure: Precision
rows.note: The authors describe this high-∆i feature as relatively selective for slang, with moderate recall.
rows.check: Precision of one SAE feature as a slang classifier. It measures register selectivity, not superposition or SAE recoverability as such.
